description: ai scientist for earth's changing surface
summary: Aletheia lets anyone ask a question about any place on Earth and get an answer measured from NISAR radar data, with receipts. You pick a place on a globe, ask in plain words and the tool reads the real NISAR files from NASA's archive and computes the answer: what changed between two dates, how a place behaved over time, or whether the ground moved. Every result comes with the files it used, its uncertainty, its caveats, and the source from how the answer was produced. NISAR passes over every place on Earth every 12 days, but its data sits in multi-gigabyte files that few people can open. Aletheia closes that gap, so that a journalist, a planner or a student can check what happened somewhere, for example after an earthquake or a hurricane, and trust the number because they can trace it.
details:
What it does. Aletheia is a web tool built on NISAR, the NASA and ISRO radar satellite. You turn a globe that shows NASA's radar picture of the Earth, click a place or search for one, and ask about it. Three analyses are available for any place NISAR has covered:

  • What changed between two dates: a map of where the ground looks different to the radar, and how much area changed. Useful for floods, water levels, logging and burns.
  • How a place behaved over time: radar brightness on every date NISAR has for it.
  • Whether the ground moved: ground movement in centimetres between two passes 12 days apart. Useful for earthquakes, volcanoes and fast sinking.

You can also ask in your own words. An investigator then chooses the analyses, runs them, looks up independent evidence such as river gauges and the earthquake record, and writes a short report that separates what was observed, what might explain it, and what the data cannot tell.

How it works. NISAR files are several gigabytes each. Aletheia does not download them. It reads only the small part of each file that covers the chosen area, directly from NASA's archive at the Alaska Satellite Facility: about 16 MB of a 7 GB file for a 10 km area. The numbers come from fixed, tested code, never from a language model. Where a language model writes the report, a check sends the report back if any figure in it cannot be traced to a computed result.

Receipts. Every result lists the exact NISAR files used, each processing step, the uncertainty, the caveats, and code that reproduces the result. Maps and data can be downloaded.

Worked examples. The site opens with three examples computed this way: the ground movement of the 24 June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela (48 to 66 cm along the radar's line of sight), the Choctawhatchee River floodplain in Florida before and after Hurricane Isaias in October 2026 (with the river gauge up 1.82 m), and Kamloops Lake through the summer of 2026 (with the river gauge down 2.97 m).

Why it matters. NISAR sees through cloud and darkness and returns to every place every 12 days, which makes it one of the best records of change on Earth. Today that record is out of reach for most people. Aletheia makes it something you can question and check.

Draft for the rest:

The idea, the scope and the decisions for this project are my own. I built it during the hackathon working with an AI coding agent (Claude Code, by Anthropic), which wrote code under my direction.

Inside the application, a language model (Qwen3 14B, run locally with Ollama; Claude is also supported) chooses which analyses to run for a question and writes the report. It does not produce numbers. Every figure is computed by fixed code reading NISAR data, and a server-side check sends back any report whose figures cannot be traced to a computed result. Text written by the model is labelled in the application.

The demo film was put together with the same AI coding agent. Every picture in it is the running application, photographed frame by frame; none of its footage is AI-generated. No images, data or measurements in the project were generated by AI.

Drafts of this page's text were prepared with AI help and edited by me.
